\chapter{Day}
\label{ch:hi-day}
\hlchaptermodality{25}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say day in Hindi and explain how \hi{दिन} both is and is not related to Latin's diēs.}

Say \hi{दिन}, put it and diēs on the same PIE *dyew- root but different branches, then name \hi{द्यु}/\hi{दिव्} as the closer cousins.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[din]{\hi{दिन} (din) — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} the same root as diēs, a different branch}

\label{lesson:HI-C25-din}



\begin{quote}
You've already met this word once, tucked inside \emph{dopahar} (\textquotedblleft{}noon,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}two pahars\textquotedblright{} of the \textbf{day}). Now it stands alone — and its connection to Latin's \emph{diēs} is real, but more careful than it first looks.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{दिन} — \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\hi{दिन}} (\textbf{din}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{} — is the ordinary Hindi word for \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} already implicit in \textbf{\hi{दोपहर}} (\emph{dopahar}, \textquotedblleft{}noon,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 17).

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The same ultimate root as diēs — but a separate branch}
\textbf{Din} traces to \textbf{Sanskrit} \textbf{\hi{दिन}} (\emph{dina}), from \textbf{Proto-Indo-Iranian} \emph{\textbf{*dinám}} — a \textbf{suffixed} formation built on \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*dyew-}} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to shine, sky}\textquotedblright{}), the same ultimate root behind \textbf{Latin}'s own \textbf{diēs}. But be careful: \emph{din} and \emph{diēs} aren't the closest possible cousins — they took \textbf{separate derivational paths} off that shared root. \emph{Din}'s own closest relatives are actually the Baltic/Slavic \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}-words, \textbf{Lithuanian} \emph{diena} and \textbf{Proto-Slavic} \emph{\textbf{*d\ru{ь}n\ru{ь}}}. The genuinely \textbf{direct}, unsuffixed cousins of \emph{diēs} are Sanskrit's own \textbf{\hi{द्यु}} (\emph{dyu}, \textquotedblleft{}heaven, sky\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\hi{दिव्}} (\emph{div}, \textquotedblleft{}sky\textquotedblright{}) — which give \textbf{\hi{दिवस}} (\emph{divasa}), yet another everyday Hindi word for \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{} So the honest picture: \emph{din} and \emph{diēs} share one distant ancestor, but \emph{dyu}/\emph{div} are the tighter match.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}din\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} already met inside dopahar
  \item the shared root — din and Latin's diēs, same PIE root \emph{dyew-}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine,\textquotedblright{} but different derivational branches
  \item the closer cousins — dyu, div, \textquotedblleft{}heaven/sky\textquotedblright{} — the tighter, unsuffixed match for diēs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where have you already met \textbf{\hi{दिन}} before this lesson? (\textbf{\hi{दोपहर}}, \emph{dopahar}, \textquotedblleft{}noon.\textquotedblright{}) What ancient PIE root connects Hindi's \textbf{din} to Latin's \textbf{diēs}, and what does it mean? (\emph{\textbf{*dyew-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine, sky\textquotedblright{} — but through \textbf{separate branches}, not as the closest cousins.) Which Sanskrit words are actually the \textbf{tighter, more direct} cousins of \emph{diēs}? (\textbf{\hi{द्यु}} \emph{dyu} and \textbf{\hi{दिव्}} \emph{div}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ga]{\hi{ग} — the other way round}

\label{lesson:HI-S138-letter-ga}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \textbf{\hi{ढ}} — how many pen lifts did it take?

That one came before any word that used it. This one comes \textbf{long after}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ग}}
\textbf{\hi{ग}} — \emph{ga}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a counterclockwise left loop joined to an ascending stem
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script: you have been reading it for twenty-two chapters}
Every one of these was yours before this page:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{स्वागत}} — the \emph{welcome} you were greeted with early on
  \item \textbf{\hi{मिलेंगे}} — \emph{we will meet}
  \item \textbf{\hi{मंगलवार}} — Tuesday
\end{itemize}

So this is the opposite arrangement from the last two letters. They arrived before their words; \textbf{this one is late, and there is no honest way to dress that up}.

The book taught its opening by \textbf{copying whole words} — a real sentence in two chapters, which is worth a great deal — and the cost is that the letters inside those words went unnamed. You have been recognising \textbf{\hi{ग}} by its company. Now you get the letter itself.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ग}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the loop's upper-right junction and sweep left over the top, down around the left side, back to the lower-right junction, and continue up the joined stem to the headline
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified three-stroke teaching form; everyday handwriting may join or simplify the body differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{ग}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 9 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words and find \hi{ग} in each one
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{स्वागत}  ·  \hi{मंगलवार}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ग} three times, saying \emph{ga} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} how long you had been reading this letter before today
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What sound does \textbf{\hi{ग}} carry? (\emph{ga}.) Name a word you have said for weeks that contains it. Why is it only being drawn now? (The opening taught whole words, so the letters inside them were never named.)
\end{tcolorbox}
